skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

4. // FrameAddress — Proofs
5. //
6. // `FrameAddress` is an immutable scalar value, so there are no state-transition
7. // lemmas. The single proof obligation that cannot be discharged from the
8. // dependency contracts alone is the *bridge* between the two projections of a
9. // `PhysicalAddress`'s abstract value:
10. //
11. //   * `PhysicalAddress`'s own `View` (`pa@`), used by `PhysicalAddress::from_number`
12. //     / `into_frame_number`; and
13. //   * the universal address projection `spec_addr(&pa)`, used by
14. //     `PageAligned::from_address` (which is generic over `T: Address` and cannot
15. //     name a per-`T` `View`).
16. //
17. // They denote the same integer; `spec_addr` is left uninterpreted only because
18. // `PageAligned<T>` is generic. The bridge lemma identifies them. Its body is
19. // `admit()` during the specification phase; the proving phase discharges it once
20. // the `Address`-trait address projection is connected to the per-type `View`.
21. 
22. verus! {
23. 
24. // Bridge: for any `PhysicalAddress`, the universal `spec_addr` projection
25. // coincides with its `View`. Used by `FrameAddress::from_frame_number` to carry
26. // `PhysicalAddress::from_number`'s `@`-based guarantee across
27. // `PageAligned::from_address`'s `spec_addr`-based contract.
28. pub proof fn lemma_phys_view_is_spec_addr(pa: PhysicalAddress)
29.     ensures
30.         crate::hal::mem::spec_addr(&pa) == pa@,
31. {
32.     admit();
33. }
34. 
35. } // verus!
36.

4. // FrameAddress — Specifications
5. //
6. // A `FrameAddress` is an opaque, page-aligned physical frame address: a `Copy`
7. // value object that names one physical frame. Its abstract value is exactly the
8. // frame's base physical address as an unbounded integer (`FrameAddress@ : int`,
9. // defined by the `View` impl below, delegating to the inner
10. // `PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>`). Callers exchange it through two equivalent
11. // identities of that single integer:
12. //
13. //   * the raw physical address — `into_raw_value` / `from_raw_value`; and
14. //   * the frame index — `into_frame_number` / `from_frame_number`, where the
15. //     index is `address / PAGE_SIZE` (`spec_frame_number`).
16. //
17. // The frame-index helpers (`spec_frame_number`, `spec_from_number`), the frame
18. // representability bound (`spec_max_frame_number`), the `arch` `FrameNumber`
19. // projection (`spec_frame_raw_value`) and the universal address projection
20. // (`spec_addr`) are all reused from the sibling `phys` / `aligned::page`
21. // specifications, so every member of the address tower speaks the same
22. // vocabulary.
23. 
24. verus! {
25. 
26. use crate::hal::mem::{
27.     spec_addr,
28.     spec_frame_number,
29.     spec_from_number,
30.     spec_frame_raw_value,
31.     spec_max_frame_number,
32. };
33. 
34. // ── Canonical page/frame size ────────────────────────────────────────────────
35. //
36. // `spec_page_size()` is the canonical frame size, re-exported from
37. // `crate::hal::mem` and shared by the whole address tower
38. // (`FRAME_SIZE == PAGE_SIZE == spec_page_size()`). It is an external-bottom
39. // trust boundary: a per-architecture runtime constant with no concrete value at
40. // the spec level. Kept here (verification material) so the exec source carries
41. // no cfg-gated verification constructs, mirroring `phys.rs`.
42. pub uninterp spec fn spec_page_size() -> int;
43. 
44. // `::arch::mem::PAGE_SIZE` is the runtime page size, tied to `spec_page_size()`.
45. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::PAGE_SIZE ] -> (result: usize)
46.     ensures
47.         result == spec_page_size(),
48. ;
49. 
50. // ── View ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
51. //
52. // `FrameAddress` abstracts to a single mathematical integer: the frame's base
53. // physical address, delegated from the inner `PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>`.
54. // `closed` so the two-level newtype delegation does not leak; callers obtain a
55. // usable `int` (`fa@`) for arithmetic, frame indexing, set membership, and
56. // comparison.
57. impl View for FrameAddress {
58.     type V = int;
59. 
60.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
61.         self.0@
62.     }
63. }
64. 
65. // ── Well-formedness invariant ────────────────────────────────────────────────
66. //
67. // Two structural guarantees every constructor establishes and callers rely on:
68. //
69. //   * page alignment (`self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`) — relied on at every MMU
70. //     / page-table / allocator site, never re-checked; and
71. //   * frame-number representability
72. //     (`spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()`) — the load-bearing
73. //     fact that makes `into_frame_number` total (its inner
74. //     `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(..).unwrap()` never panics) and lets the frame
75. //     allocator use the result directly as a bitmap / refcount index.
76. //
77. // Stated purely over the abstract address `self@`, independent of the inner
78. // representation.
79. impl FrameAddress {
80.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
81.         &&& self@ % spec_page_size() == 0
82.         &&& spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()
83.     }
84. }
85. 
86. // ── `hal::mem` library-edge trust boundary ───────────────────────────────────
87. //
88. // `<PhysicalAddress as Address>::from_raw_value` is a method of the external
89. // `sys::mm::Address` trait, below this module's verification boundary; a
90. // trait-impl method cannot be body-verified in place without marking the whole
91. // `impl Address for PhysicalAddress` verified (pulling its unsupported
92. // `usize as *const u8` sibling casts into scope — see
93. // `verus-ai-logs/verus-unsupported.md`). It is therefore specced here with
94. // `assume_specification`, mirroring the trust boundary the codebase already
95. // draws for `<PageAligned<T> as Address>::into_raw_value` (`page.spec.rs`) and
96. // `::arch::mem::PAGE_SIZE` (above).
97. //
98. // On success it validates and wraps without rounding: the abstract address
99. // equals the raw value (`r@ == value`) and the validated address has a
100. // representable frame number (`spec_frame_number(r@) <= spec_max_frame_number()`,
101. // i.e. it lies within physical memory). On failure (`value` is not a valid
102. // physical address) no address is produced; the dynamic validity predicate is
103. // platform-specific, so the failure condition is left unconstrained —
104. // `from_raw_value`'s sole caller only branches on `Ok`/`Err`. Stated through
105. // `PhysicalAddress`'s `View` (`r@`) rather than the universal `spec_addr` to
106. // avoid a definitional cycle (`spec_addr<PhysicalAddress>` would depend back on
107. // the very `impl Address for PhysicalAddress` this method belongs to);
108. // `FrameAddress::from_raw_value` bridges `r@` to `spec_addr` in its body.
109. // Removed when `hal::mem` is verified.
110. pub assume_specification[ <PhysicalAddress as Address>::from_raw_value ](
111.     value: usize,
112. ) -> (result: Result<PhysicalAddress, ::sys::error::Error>)
113.     ensures
114.         match result {
115.             Ok(r) => r@ == value as int
116.                 && spec_frame_number(r@) <= spec_max_frame_number(),
117.             Err(_) => true,
118.         },
119. ;
120. 
121. // `<PageAligned<T> as Deref>::deref` is the auto-deref that resolves
122. // `self.0.into_frame_number()` to `PhysicalAddress::into_frame_number`. It is a
123. // trait-impl method of the external `core::ops::Deref` trait, below this
124. // module's verification boundary, specced here as a trust boundary. It is pure
125. // projection: the borrowed inner address has the same abstract value as the
126. // wrapper (`spec_addr(result) == addr@`). Stated through the universal
127. // `spec_addr` projection rather than `result@`, because a bare `T: Address`
128. // carries no `View<V = int>` bound (mirrors `page.spec.rs`).
129. pub assume_specification<T: Address> [
130.     <PageAligned<T> as ::core::ops::Deref>::deref
131. ](addr: &PageAligned<T>) -> (result: &<PageAligned<T> as ::core::ops::Deref>::Target)
132.     ensures
133.         spec_addr(result) == addr@,
134. ;
135. 
136. } // verus!
137.

`frame.rs` is now the proof target. Two layers form the trust boundary of the
global frame-allocator singleton; everything else in the module (the `frame::*`
free-function shims) is **body-verified** against these contracts.

### 1. The singleton bridge: `instance()`

`instance()` returns `&'static mut Inner` obtained from the module-level

does not support `static mut` paths, and a zero-argument uninterpreted

is therefore the bridge axiom: `requires phys_view().initialized` (the real panic
gate) and `ensures (*result).inv() && (*result)@ == phys_view().frames`. This is
what lets the query shims (`is_covered`, `refcount`) be fully body-verified.

  bridges the live `Inner` to the abstract `phys_view().frames`.

transition contract, but its **body** cannot be translated by Verus: every method
uses the `error!` / `debug_assert_eq!` macros (whose expansion needs
`core::fmt::Arguments`, unsupported — the same limitation already recorded for
`UserFrame::drop`) and the `arch` newtypes `FrameNumber` / `FrameAddress`
(external types with no `external_type_specification`). They are `external_body`
with their pre-existing `#[verus_spec]` contracts honored as trust boundaries.

- `Inner::alloc`, `Inner::alloc_contiguous`, `Inner::free`, `Inner::share`,
  `Inner::refcount`, `Inner::book`, `Inner::is_covered`, `Inner::alloc_range`
  (all in `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs`).

The `frame::*` free-function shims are no longer `external_body`. The pure-query
shims `is_covered` and `refcount` are proven outright via the `instance()` bridge.
The aggregate query shim `free_count` is also fully body-verified via
`lemma_free_count` (`frame.proof.rs`): it counts the clear bitmap indices as the
image of an injective `i -> i * page_size` map and discharges
`free_frames.len() + usage == num_bits` without any `admit()`.

The mutating reservation shims (`alloc`, `alloc_contiguous`, `book`,
`alloc_range`, `share`) are body-verified and carry the **strong** post-state
contract via the `tracked PhysAuth` carrier threaded through `&mut`: each names
both `old(auth)@` (pre-state) and `final(auth)@` (post-state) and asserts the
exact `FrameAllocView` transition (`spec_alloc_one` / `spec_alloc_set` /
`spec_share`), with a meaningful `Err` arm (`final(auth)@ == old(auth)@`). They
carry no `admit()`.

trait-fixed `drop(&mut self)` signature is `opens_invariants none` + `no_unwind`,

**cannot** open a global invariant to reach the authority. Without the token the
body cannot discharge `instance()`'s `phys_view().initialized` precondition nor

precondition-free for `Drop` soundness. The function is therefore `external_body`

that now carry the strong `PhysAuth`-threaded post-state.

  `ensures phys_view().inv()` on every path; no precondition (`Drop`-safe).

`UserFrame::drop` releases the frame's reference by calling `frame::free` and, on

`core::fmt` Debug formatting (`{:?}`), which Verus cannot translate to VIR
("Unsupported constant type"). The function is therefore `external_body`; its

new guarantee — `ensures phys_view().inv()` is exactly the post-state already
established by the `external_body` `frame::free` shim it calls, and the logging
branch performs no state change. `opens_invariants none` / `no_unwind` record that
`drop` opens no invariant and cannot unwind (errors are logged, not propagated).

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/upool.rs::<UserFrame as Drop>::drop` — releases one
  reference on scope exit. `ensures phys_view().inv()` on every path.

`PhysMemoryManager` is a **stateless facade** over the global frame allocator
(`Upool` has no fields; kernel frames are drawn from the global `frame::*`
statics through `static mut PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER`). Its target methods therefore

ghost-gated and have no `vstd` specs. They form a trust boundary identical in

contract stated over the do-not-modify `phys_view()` / `FrameAllocView` and the
returned frame values (monotone post-state facts, as there is no
`old(phys_view())`). Abstract laws are carried by `manager.proof.rs` lemmas.

  global `static mut PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER` (`MaybeUninit::write`) and flips an
  `AtomicBool`. `ensures` keeps the allocator initialized and well-formed.

===== verus-constraints =====
---
name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers verus! block syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## verus! { } Blocks Only

All spec and proof code **must** use native `verus! { }` block syntax.
Do **not** use attribute-based syntax (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`).

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!

// ❌ WRONG — attribute style
#[verus_spec(ret => requires x < 100, ensures ret == x + 1)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 { x + 1 }
```

Even if existing code uses attribute style, write all new code in `verus! { }` style.
Attribute style is less mature; `verus! { }` can be auto-converted later.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Do not change
code logic; keep changes minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions, comments,
debug assertions, and all other existing code. If a construct is unsupported by
Verus (e.g. `debug_assert!`), cfg-gate it with `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]`
rather than deleting.

**Allowed additions:** `verus! { }` blocks (requires, ensures, invariants, decreases,
proof blocks, assert), vstd imports (cfg-gated), named returns `-> (ret: T)`,
ghost/tracked variables, `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**Never change:** semantic code logic or function/struct signatures. Exception:
only if Verus genuinely cannot express a construct — first search vstd for
alternatives, build a minimal reproducer proving unsupported, then make the
smallest change needed and document why.

**Iterator rewrite rule:** When exec code uses Iterator chains
(`.iter().filter().map().collect()`), these MUST be rewritten to while
loops because Iterator API is unsupported. This is a permitted exec
change because: (1) the behavioral semantics are identical, (2) it is
a true Verus limitation, (3) the ensures should describe the ORIGINAL
functional intent using `Seq::filter`/`Seq::map_values`, not the
rewritten loop structure.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in initial skeleton proofs |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | Banned **as a workaround** for spec/proof difficulty. Permitted ONLY for functions that use a True Limitation feature (async, float arithmetic, transmute, static mut) — see True Limitations table below. If the function body is pure Rust with supported types, it MUST be verified, not escaped. |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |

## assume_specification — Human-Approved Only

`assume_specification` and `axiom` are **external-bottom** trust
assumptions (see **spec-design** skill, Part 2). They introduce
unverified axioms — if wrong, the entire verification is unsound.

`external_type_specification` is safe to use freely — it only declares
that a type exists without introducing logical assumptions.

**You must NOT write `assume_specification` or `axiom` yourself** unless
a human has explicitly approved them (e.g., via checked items in the
property analysis). If you discover a missing assumption, report it and
use `admit()` as a temporary placeholder.

**Before reporting:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

Before writing custom specs, search vstd for existing ones (sequences, sets,
maps, arithmetic, pointers, atomics).

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

## False Limitations (v0.2026.04.03)

The following features **work** in current Verus. Do NOT claim they are unsupported:

| Feature | Status | Notes |
|---------|--------|-------|
| `dyn trait` (basic + Box\<dyn\>) | ✅ Works | Including trait with spec methods |
| `DerefMut` / `v[i] = x` on `&mut Vec` | ✅ Works | Use `v.set(i, x)` |
| Multiple `&mut` params (`swap(a, b)`) | ✅ Works | `old(a)`, `old(b)` in ensures |
| `std::collections::HashMap` (basic) | ✅ Works | `new()`, `insert()` verified |
| `Box::new` with ensures | ✅ Works | `ensures *b == 42` |
| `Option::unwrap_or` | ✅ Works | |
| Nested `proof fn` calls (3+ layers) | ✅ Works | |
| `for` loop with `iter:` | ✅ Works | |
| `const fn` | ✅ Works | Needs overflow handling |
| Recursive types (`Box<Self>`) | ✅ Works | Add `decreases self` |
| `type_invariant` | ✅ Works | Use `proof { use_type_invariant(self); }` |
| `broadcast proof/use` | ✅ Works | |
| `Seq::filter` / `Seq::map_values` in spec | ✅ Works | Exec needs loop, but spec can use these |

## Spec Vocabulary Reference

When writing spec, you have these tools. Each includes **when to use** (not just what it is):

**choose:** `choose|x: T| P(x)` — Use when you have `exists|x| P(x)` and need a concrete witness value in a spec expression. Without this, you cannot define spec functions that "pick" a satisfying element.

**Extensional equality:** `=~=` for Seq/Set/Map, `=~~=` for nested collections. In many simple cases `==` also works for Seq, but when Z3 struggles with collection equality, switch to `=~=`. **Guideline: start with `==`, use `=~=` if Z3 can't prove it.**

**old():** `old(self)@` in ensures of `&mut` functions. **Test: does this function take &mut? Then ensures MUST contain old().** Without this, ensures compares new state to itself (tautological).

**ghost struct:** Use when you need a spec-only abstraction that has no exec counterpart. Example: an `Interval { lo: int, hi: int }` for reasoning about address ranges that don't exist as a runtime type.

**spec_fn:** `spec_fn(T) -> U` — Use when a spec needs to be parameterized by a function. Example: a generic "map" spec that takes a transformation function.

**Seq operations in spec:** Even though `Iterator` chains are not available in exec, `Seq` provides the same operations in spec: `s.filter(|x| p(x))`, `s.map_values(|x| f(x))`, `s.subrange(lo, hi)`, `s.update(i, x)`, `s.contains(x)`. **When exec uses a while loop to implement filter/map, the ensures should still use Seq::filter/map_values to express the intent declaratively.**

**Map::dom():** Returns `Set<K>`. Use for "all keys satisfy P": `forall|k| m.dom().contains(k) ==> P(m[k])`. Without this, you can't quantify over Map keys.

## True Limitations (cannot work around in spec)

| Feature | Impact on Spec |
|---------|---------------|
| `async fn` / `await` | Cannot write requires/ensures. Must use `#[verifier::external]`. |
| `f32`/`f64` arithmetic in spec | Cannot reason about float results. |
| `static mut` | No spec model. |
| `transmute` | No spec model. |
===== proving-guide =====
---
name: proving-guide
description: "Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures."
---

# Proving Guide

Read `verus-constraints` first. Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/`
for a working example.

## Core Approach

1. **One function at a time.** Resolve `admit()` function by function. Do not
   move to the next function until the current one verifies cleanly.

2. **Keep trying.** When verification fails, read the error log carefully,
   try a different proof strategy, and iterate. You are capable of solving
   this — if one approach fails, try the next. Do not give up or ask for
   suggestions; work through possible approaches systematically.

3. **Report genuine bugs.** If after thorough attempts you determine the
   failure is caused by a code bug (not a proof gap), report it immediately
   using the `bug-reporting` skill. Do not silently work around code bugs.

4. **Clean verification.** After all proofs pass, check for warnings and
   resolve them. A clean verification has zero errors AND zero warnings.

## Verification Tool

Use `make verify-<crate> MODULE=<module>` to verify the current module during
proving. After all modules are done, run `make verify-<crate>` (no MODULE) to
confirm the full crate still passes. The output includes:
- **Verification result** — pass/fail with error details
- **Cheating detection** — flags `admit`, `assume`, `external_body`, `trusted`;
  all cheating must be resolved before the proof is considered complete
- **Coverage** — which functions have contracts

After verification passes, use the `ast-consistency` skill to check that
exec code was not accidentally modified during proving. Fix all
inconsistencies before finalizing.

name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers verus! block syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## verus! { } Blocks Only

All spec and proof code **must** use native `verus! { }` block syntax.
Do **not** use attribute-based syntax (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`).

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!

// ❌ WRONG — attribute style
#[verus_spec(ret => requires x < 100, ensures ret == x + 1)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 { x + 1 }
```

Even if existing code uses attribute style, write all new code in `verus! { }` style.
Attribute style is less mature; `verus! { }` can be auto-converted later.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Do not change
code logic; keep changes minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions, comments,
debug assertions, and all other existing code. If a construct is unsupported by
Verus (e.g. `debug_assert!`), cfg-gate it with `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]`
rather than deleting.

**Allowed additions:** `verus! { }` blocks (requires, ensures, invariants, decreases,
proof blocks, assert), vstd imports (cfg-gated), named returns `-> (ret: T)`,
ghost/tracked variables, `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**Never change:** semantic code logic or function/struct signatures. Exception:
only if Verus genuinely cannot express a construct — first search vstd for
alternatives, build a minimal reproducer proving unsupported, then make the
smallest change needed and document why.

**Iterator rewrite rule:** When exec code uses Iterator chains
(`.iter().filter().map().collect()`), these MUST be rewritten to while
loops because Iterator API is unsupported. This is a permitted exec
change because: (1) the behavioral semantics are identical, (2) it is
a true Verus limitation, (3) the ensures should describe the ORIGINAL
functional intent using `Seq::filter`/`Seq::map_values`, not the
rewritten loop structure.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in initial skeleton proofs |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | Banned **as a workaround** for spec/proof difficulty. Permitted ONLY for functions that use a True Limitation feature (async, float arithmetic, transmute, static mut) — see True Limitations table below. If the function body is pure Rust with supported types, it MUST be verified, not escaped. |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |

## assume_specification — Human-Approved Only

`assume_specification` and `axiom` are **external-bottom** trust
assumptions (see **spec-design** skill, Part 2). They introduce
unverified axioms — if wrong, the entire verification is unsound.

`external_type_specification` is safe to use freely — it only declares
that a type exists without introducing logical assumptions.

**You must NOT write `assume_specification` or `axiom` yourself** unless
a human has explicitly approved them (e.g., via checked items in the
property analysis). If you discover a missing assumption, report it and
use `admit()` as a temporary placeholder.

**Before reporting:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

Before writing custom specs, search vstd for existing ones (sequences, sets,
maps, arithmetic, pointers, atomics).

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

## False Limitations (v0.2026.04.03)

The following features **work** in current Verus. Do NOT claim they are unsupported:

| Feature | Status | Notes |
|---------|--------|-------|
| `dyn trait` (basic + Box\<dyn\>) | ✅ Works | Including trait with spec methods |
| `DerefMut` / `v[i] = x` on `&mut Vec` | ✅ Works | Use `v.set(i, x)` |
| Multiple `&mut` params (`swap(a, b)`) | ✅ Works | `old(a)`, `old(b)` in ensures |
| `std::collections::HashMap` (basic) | ✅ Works | `new()`, `insert()` verified |
| `Box::new` with ensures | ✅ Works | `ensures *b == 42` |
| `Option::unwrap_or` | ✅ Works | |
| Nested `proof fn` calls (3+ layers) | ✅ Works | |
| `for` loop with `iter:` | ✅ Works | |
| `const fn` | ✅ Works | Needs overflow handling |
| Recursive types (`Box<Self>`) | ✅ Works | Add `decreases self` |
| `type_invariant` | ✅ Works | Use `proof { use_type_invariant(self); }` |
| `broadcast proof/use` | ✅ Works | |
| `Seq::filter` / `Seq::map_values` in spec | ✅ Works | Exec needs loop, but spec can use these |

## Spec Vocabulary Reference

When writing spec, you have these tools. Each includes **when to use** (not just what it is):

**choose:** `choose|x: T| P(x)` — Use when you have `exists|x| P(x)` and need a concrete witness value in a spec expression. Without this, you cannot define spec functions that "pick" a satisfying element.

**Extensional equality:** `=~=` for Seq/Set/Map, `=~~=` for nested collections. In many simple cases `==` also works for Seq, but when Z3 struggles with collection equality, switch to `=~=`. **Guideline: start with `==`, use `=~=` if Z3 can't prove it.**

**old():** `old(self)@` in ensures of `&mut` functions. **Test: does this function take &mut? Then ensures MUST contain old().** Without this, ensures compares new state to itself (tautological).

**ghost struct:** Use when you need a spec-only abstraction that has no exec counterpart. Example: an `Interval { lo: int, hi: int }` for reasoning about address ranges that don't exist as a runtime type.

**spec_fn:** `spec_fn(T) -> U` — Use when a spec needs to be parameterized by a function. Example: a generic "map" spec that takes a transformation function.

**Seq operations in spec:** Even though `Iterator` chains are not available in exec, `Seq` provides the same operations in spec: `s.filter(|x| p(x))`, `s.map_values(|x| f(x))`, `s.subrange(lo, hi)`, `s.update(i, x)`, `s.contains(x)`. **When exec uses a while loop to implement filter/map, the ensures should still use Seq::filter/map_values to express the intent declaratively.**

**Map::dom():** Returns `Set<K>`. Use for "all keys satisfy P": `forall|k| m.dom().contains(k) ==> P(m[k])`. Without this, you can't quantify over Map keys.

## True Limitations (cannot work around in spec)

| Feature | Impact on Spec |
|---------|---------------|
| `async fn` / `await` | Cannot write requires/ensures. Must use `#[verifier::external]`. |
| `f32`/`f64` arithmetic in spec | Cannot reason about float results. |
| `static mut` | No spec model. |
| `transmute` | No spec model. |

name: proving-guide
description: "Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures."
---

# Proving Guide

Read `verus-constraints` first. Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/`
for a working example.

## Core Approach

1. **One function at a time.** Resolve `admit()` function by function. Do not
   move to the next function until the current one verifies cleanly.

2. **Keep trying.** When verification fails, read the error log carefully,
   try a different proof strategy, and iterate. You are capable of solving
   this — if one approach fails, try the next. Do not give up or ask for
   suggestions; work through possible approaches systematically.

3. **Report genuine bugs.** If after thorough attempts you determine the
   failure is caused by a code bug (not a proof gap), report it immediately
   using the `bug-reporting` skill. Do not silently work around code bugs.

4. **Clean verification.** After all proofs pass, check for warnings and
   resolve them. A clean verification has zero errors AND zero warnings.

## Verification Tool

Use `make verify-<crate> MODULE=<module>` to verify the current module during
proving. After all modules are done, run `make verify-<crate>` (no MODULE) to
confirm the full crate still passes. The output includes:
- **Verification result** — pass/fail with error details
- **Cheating detection** — flags `admit`, `assume`, `external_body`, `trusted`;
  all cheating must be resolved before the proof is considered complete
- **Coverage** — which functions have contracts

After verification passes, use the `ast-consistency` skill to check that
exec code was not accidentally modified during proving. Fix all
inconsistencies before finalizing.

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## verus! { } Blocks Only

All spec and proof code **must** use native `verus! { }` block syntax.
Do **not** use attribute-based syntax (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`).

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!

// ❌ WRONG — attribute style
#[verus_spec(ret => requires x < 100, ensures ret == x + 1)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 { x + 1 }
```

Even if existing code uses attribute style, write all new code in `verus! { }` style.
Attribute style is less mature; `verus! { }` can be auto-converted later.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Do not change
code logic; keep changes minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions, comments,
debug assertions, and all other existing code. If a construct is unsupported by
Verus (e.g. `debug_assert!`), cfg-gate it with `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]`
rather than deleting.

**Allowed additions:** `verus! { }` blocks (requires, ensures, invariants, decreases,
proof blocks, assert), vstd imports (cfg-gated), named returns `-> (ret: T)`,
ghost/tracked variables, `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**Never change:** semantic code logic or function/struct signatures. Exception:
only if Verus genuinely cannot express a construct — first search vstd for
alternatives, build a minimal reproducer proving unsupported, then make the
smallest change needed and document why.

**Iterator rewrite rule:** When exec code uses Iterator chains
(`.iter().filter().map().collect()`), these MUST be rewritten to while
loops because Iterator API is unsupported. This is a permitted exec
change because: (1) the behavioral semantics are identical, (2) it is
a true Verus limitation, (3) the ensures should describe the ORIGINAL
functional intent using `Seq::filter`/`Seq::map_values`, not the
rewritten loop structure.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must

is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented.

| Pattern | Policy |

| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in initial skeleton proofs |

| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |

`assume_specification` and `axiom` are **external-bottom** trust
assumptions (see **spec-design** skill, Part 2). They introduce
unverified axioms — if wrong, the entire verification is unsound.

`external_type_specification` is safe to use freely — it only declares
that a type exists without introducing logical assumptions.

a human has explicitly approved them (e.g., via checked items in the
property analysis). If you discover a missing assumption, report it and
use `admit()` as a temporary placeholder.

**Before reporting:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

Before writing custom specs, search vstd for existing ones (sequences, sets,
maps, arithmetic, pointers, atomics).

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

cannot be proven correct and should not be. Ask: "Is this ensures what I
actually want? Does it match the function's documented behavior?" Only
after confirming the spec is correct should you add proof hints.

Every function that can fail should specify **what happens on failure**
with the same rigor as the success path.

1. **State Preservation** — on error, the state must not change.
2. **Bidirectional Failure Condition** — specify *when* it fails (iff),
   not just *that* it can fail.
3. **Liveness** — when preconditions guarantee success, state it
   explicitly. Even if logically derivable from the bidirectional
   condition, an explicit liveness ensures aids caller reasoning.
4. **Specific Error Identification** — each error branch should be
   distinguishable by its postcondition.

**Completely skip** (no spec needed at all):
- **Type-system guarantees** — ownership, borrow rules, type matching
- **Display/formatting** — debug output, logging, string representation
- **Boilerplate trait impls** — derived traits, mechanical delegations

**Basic ensures only** (no additional spec design):
- **Trivial accessors** — field getters still need
  `ensures result == self@.field` for callers to reason about, but
  warrant no further properties.
- **Pure wrappers** — functions that directly delegate to a single
  verified function with no additional logic.

### Static vs Dynamic Condition Enforcement

**Key question**: Can this runtime check be statically eliminated through
verification?

**Yes → add `requires`**. The condition is provable from caller context
(e.g., index bounds derived from loop invariants, capacity checked before
insertion). The runtime check serves as a safeguard during development;
once all callers are verified, it becomes dead code and can be removed.

**No → keep runtime check + Err**. The condition depends on inherently
dynamic information (external input, hardware state, concurrent
operations) that no amount of static reasoning can discharge. A
`requires` clause here would be unsound or unusable.

**Guideline**: When both `requires` and a runtime check coexist, the
runtime check is a temporary safety net. Mark it as removable (e.g.,

verification work knows to clean it up.

Specifications fall into three categories with different ownership:

### Internal

Specs that exist solely to help the verifier: helper lemmas, loop
invariants, intermediate assertions, proof-function pre/postconditions.

correctness is whether the code above can use them — the verifier
provides direct feedback.

### External-top (API contracts)

Public function `requires`/`ensures`, type invariants exposed to
callers, View types. These define **what the module promises**.

Understandability is critical — a human auditor who cannot understand
the spec cannot approve it.

### External-bottom (trust assumptions)

below (stdlib, hardware, FFI). **These are trust boundaries: if wrong,
everything above is unsound.** Only a human may approve these. The AI
must never write them on its own — if it discovers a need, it must
report it and wait for human approval.

without introducing logical assumptions.)

### Internal

Specs that exist solely to help the verifier: helper lemmas, loop
invariants, intermediate assertions, proof-function pre/postconditions.
**The AI generates these freely during proving.** The test for
correctness is whether the code above can use them — the verifier
provides direct feedback.

### External-top (API contracts)

Public function `requires`/`ensures`, type invariants exposed to
callers, View types. These define **what the module promises**.
A human must review them for correctness and completeness.
Understandability is critical — a human auditor who cannot understand
the spec cannot approve it.

### External-bottom (trust assumptions)

`assume_specification` and `axiom` — assumptions about unverified layers
below (stdlib, hardware, FFI). **These are trust boundaries: if wrong,
everything above is unsound.** Only a human may approve these. The AI
must never write them on its own — if it discovers a need, it must
report it and wait for human approval.

(`external_type_specification` is safe — it only declares a type exists
without introducing logical assumptions.)

### Rules

- Property analysis identifies external-top properties and reports
  needed external-bottom assumptions as a checklist (without writing code).
- A human reviews the checklist: approve items by checking them,
  reject by leaving unchecked, and optionally add notes or extra
  assumptions.
- Only approved assumptions may be turned into `assume_specification` /
  `axiom` code. Any unapproved use is treated as cheating.

---

## Part 3: View Abstraction Design

See `docs/specifying-and-proving-types.md` for a detailed step-by-step guide.

### View Design Principles

1. **Only caller-visible state** — hide internal bookkeeping (caches,
   auxiliary indices, raw pointers). **Judgment method: look at the
   public API methods. What state do they expose through their return
   values and ensures? That state belongs in View. Internal fields that
   no public method references do not.** Test: if you swapped the
   underlying data structure, would the View fields still make sense?
2. **`view()` is `pub closed spec fn`** — public so callers can invoke it,
   closed so implementation details don't leak.
3. **No extra pub spec fns on `impl MyType`** beyond `inv` and `view`.
   Put reusable spec helpers on `MyTypeView` instead, so callers reason
   about the abstraction, not the concrete type.

### Spec Transition Functions

For each state-mutating exec function, define a corresponding spec function
on the View type. Use `..self` to implicitly preserve unchanged fields
(frame condition):

```rust
impl FooView {
    pub open spec fn spec_insert(self, elem: int) -> FooView {
        FooView { elements: self.elements.insert(elem), ..self }
    }
}
// ensures self@ == old(self)@.spec_insert(elem as int)
```

**Do NOT** also list individual field changes as separate ensures — the
spec transition already captures the complete state change.

When modifying a collection element without a spec transition, state the
frame explicitly:
`forall|i: int| i != changed_idx ==> new@[i] == old@[i]`

## Exec → Spec Conversion for Unsupported APIs

When exec code uses an unsupported API, the **spec** can still capture the full semantics.
The exec code must be rewritten, but the ensures should express the original intent:

| Exec Pattern | Rewrite Exec To | Ensures Uses |
|-------------|----------------|-------------|
| `v.iter().filter(\|x\| p(x)).collect()` | `while` loop + `if p(v[i])` | `result@ == v@.filter(\|x\| p_spec(x))` |
| `v.iter().map(\|x\| f(x)).collect()` | `while` loop + `result.push(f(v[i]))` | `result@ == v@.map_values(\|x\| f_spec(x))` |
| `v.iter().any(\|x\| p(x))` | `while` loop + early return | `result == v@.filter(\|x\| p_spec(x)).len() > 0` |
| `v.sort()` | manual sort or external_body | `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation(result@, old(v)@)` |
| `cell.set(x)` | `pcell.put(Tracked(&mut perm), x)` | `perm.value() == x` |

**Key insight:** `Seq::filter` and `Seq::map_values` are available in spec/ensures
even though `Iterator` is not available in exec. Never weaken the ensures just
because the exec API changed.

## Deeper Spec Design Decisions

The principles above tell you what good spec looks like. These address
**judgment calls** that require deeper reasoning:

### View abstraction level

View should model the **interface**, not the **implementation**.
Test: if two implementations (HashMap, BTreeMap) provide the same
public API, they should have the same View (Map<K,V>). If your View
exposes implementation details (hash buckets, tree nodes), it is
too concrete.

### Invariant strength

An invariant should be exactly strong enough to imply all ensures
clauses, and no stronger. Too weak: proof cannot go through.
Too strong: invariant itself is unprovable.

Start from ensures, work backwards: what must be true at every
point for ensures to hold at the end? That is your invariant.

### When to use spec transition functions

Use a spec transition function (`spec fn spec_insert(self, ...) -> Self`)
when a mutation changes multiple fields with inter-dependent constraints.
The transition function captures the state change atomically.

For single-field changes, write ensures directly:
`ensures self@.count == old(self)@.count + 1`.

### Quantifier style: index vs membership

Use **index quantifiers** (`forall|i: int| 0 <= i < s.len() ==> P(s[i])`)
when the property depends on position (ordering, adjacency).

Use **membership quantifiers** (`forall|x| s.contains(x) ==> P(x)`)
when only the element value matters, not its position.

Prefer index quantifiers when in doubt — they are more trigger-friendly
(s[i] is a clean trigger) and more general.

### When to introduce helper spec functions

Extract a helper when:
1. The same expression appears in requires + ensures + invariant
   (DRY: spec should not repeat itself)
2. A quantifier needs a trigger-friendly wrapper for arithmetic
   indexing (e.g., `spec fn at_offset(s, i, j) -> T { s[i + j] }`)
3. A complex predicate deserves a name for readability
   (e.g., `spec fn is_sorted(s: Seq<int>) -> bool`)

Do NOT extract a helper just to shorten one ensures clause.
Helpers add indirection; only use when reuse or triggers justify it.

### Requires strength: weakest precondition

requires should be the **weakest condition under which the function
behaves correctly**. Do not over-constrain.

- Too strong: `requires v.len() == 10` when the function works for any length.
  This prevents callers from using the function on shorter vectors.
- Too weak: `requires true` when the function can overflow on large inputs.
  This makes the proof fail inside the function body.
- Just right: `requires v.len() <= MAX` where MAX is the actual bound
  needed for overflow safety.

**Test:** for each requires clause, ask "if I removed this, would the
function still be correct for some inputs?" If yes, the clause may
be too strong. If the function crashes without it, it is necessary.

### Spec vocabulary consistency across a module

All functions on the same struct/type should use the **same View type,
same helper spec functions, and same way of referencing state**. If
`insert` uses `self@.map.contains_key(k)` then `remove` must also use
`self@.map` — not `self@.data@.contains(k)` through a different path.

Inconsistency makes caller reasoning impossible: the caller cannot
chain `insert` ensures into `remove` requires if they speak different
spec languages.

**Test:** read all ensures on the same struct. Do they use the same
View fields and helper functions? If not, unify them.

name: bug-reporting
description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."

# Bug Reporting

Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.

## Classification

After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:

**True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
logic error that always produces wrong results).

**Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.

**False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).

## When to Report

- **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
- **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
  needed and where they might come from.
- **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
  Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
  failure; see `verus-constraints`.

## Report Format

Write findings to the bugs file (path provided in prompt context).
Reports will be read by human developers — use clear language, avoid jargon,
and make each report self-contained so readers need no additional context.

```markdown
## [True Bug | Context-Dependent] — function_name (file.rs:line)

**What**: one-line summary of the issue.
**Why**: root cause analysis — what the code does wrong and why.
**Verification Failure**: which clause failed (requires/ensures/invariant/assert),
verification command, and key error output.
**How Verus Helped**: how formal verification caught this bug (e.g. would it
be caught by testing? code review? why verification was uniquely effective).
**Severity**: safety-critical / correctness / cosmetic.
**Suggested Fix**: how the code should be changed.
```

If no bugs are found, write "None" to the bugs file.

70. pub open spec fn spec_from_number(frame_view: int) -> int {
71.     frame_view * spec_page_size()
72. }
73. 
74. // ── `arch`/`sys` library-edge `assume_specification`s ─────────────────────────
75. 
76. // `::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE` is the frame size (alias of `PAGE_SIZE`), tied to the
77. // canonical `spec_page_size()`. It is strictly positive (`== 4096`); positivity is
78. // the load-bearing fact for the division/modulo reasoning in the constructors.
79. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE ] -> (result: usize)
80.     ensures
81.         result == spec_page_size(),
82.         spec_page_size() > 0,
83. ;
84. 
85. // `::arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT == log2(FRAME_SIZE)`. Bounded below the pointer width
86. // so `raw_addr >> FRAME_SHIFT` is well-defined, and `2^FRAME_SHIFT == FRAME_SIZE`
87. // so the shift coincides with division by `spec_page_size()`.
88. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT ] -> (result: usize)
89.     ensures
90.         result < usize::BITS,
91.         pow2(result as nat) == spec_page_size(),
92. ;
93. 
94. // `VirtualAddress::new` now carries a native `#[verus_spec]` in `sys`
95. // (`mm::address::virt`), so its contract is imported directly across the crate
96. // boundary; a local `assume_specification` here would duplicate it (Verus error:
97. // "duplicate specification for ... ::new"). The guaranteed fact is identical
98. // (`result@ == value as int`).
99. 
100. // `<VirtualAddress as Address>::into_raw_value` is pure newtype identity: the
101. // returned raw `usize` equals the abstract address. It remains an
102. // `assume_specification` trust boundary because this trait-impl method cannot be
103. // body-verified in `sys` without marking the whole `impl Address for
104. // VirtualAddress` verified, which pulls the sibling `as_ptr`/`as_mut_ptr` methods
105. // (unsupported `usize as *const u8` casts) into scope — a Verus front-end
106. // limitation (see `verus-ai-logs/verus-unsupported.md`).
107. pub assume_specification[ <VirtualAddress as Address>::into_raw_value ](
108.     addr: VirtualAddress,
109. ) -> (result: usize)
110.     ensures
111.         result as int == addr@,
112. ;
113. 
114. // `FrameNumber::into_raw_value` projects a frame number to its index; every
115. // `FrameNumber` value is in range (`0 ..= MAX`) by construction.
116. pub assume_specification[ FrameNumber::into_raw_value ](frame: FrameNumber) -> (result: usize)
117.     ensures
118.         result as int == spec_frame_raw_value(frame),
119.         0 <= spec_frame_raw_value(frame) <= spec_max_frame_number(),
120. ;
121. 
122. // `FrameNumber::from_raw_value` succeeds iff `value <= MAX`, preserving the index.
123. pub assume_specification[ FrameNumber::from_raw_value ](value: usize) -> (result: Option<FrameNumber>)
124.     ensures
125.         match result {
126.             Some(f) => value as int <= spec_max_frame_number()
127.                 && spec_frame_raw_value(f) == value as int,
128.             None => value as int > spec_max_frame_number(),
129.         },
130. ;
131. 
132. // ── Type invariant ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
133. //
134. // Every `PhysicalAddress` a verified constructor produces has a *representable
135. // frame number*: `self@ / FRAME_SIZE <= FrameNumber::MAX`. This is the load-
136. // bearing fact that makes `into_frame_number` total (its internal
137. // `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(..).unwrap()` never panics), which the frame
138. // allocator relies on when using the result directly as a bitmap / refcount
139. // index. It is *not* alignment (MMIO addresses may be unaligned) and *not*
140. // RAM-validity (`from_mmio_address` deliberately bypasses that check).
141. impl PhysicalAddress {
142.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
143.         spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()
144.     }
145. }
146. 
147. // `PhysicalAddress` abstracts to a single mathematical integer: the raw physical
148. // address, delegated from the inner `VirtualAddress`. Kept here (verification
149. // material) rather than in `phys.rs` so the exec source carries no cfg-gated
150. // verification constructs.
151. impl View for PhysicalAddress {
152.     type V = int;
153. 
154.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
155.         self.0@
156.     }
157. }
158. 
159. } // verus!
160.

4. // PageAligned<T> — Specifications
5. //
6. // `PageAligned<T>` is a validated newtype wrapping a memory address (`int`)
7. // carrying the static guarantee that the address lies on a page boundary. Its
8. // abstract value is exactly that address (`PageAligned@ : int`, defined by the
9. // `View` impl in `page.rs`); the page-alignment fact is the property `inv()`
10. // over that value.
11. //
12. // `spec_addr` is the ghost projection of an arbitrary `T: Address` to its
13. // abstract address (`int`). It exists for *every* `T: Address` so that the
14. // `View` impl for `PageAligned<T>` — and hence the `@`-based contracts of the
15. // in-scope exec functions (`into_raw_value`, `from_address`) — can be stated
16. // for a bare `T: Address`, without the `T: View<V = int>` bound that would
17. //   * be unsatisfiable in a normal `cargo build` (the address-family `View`
18. //     impls are all `cfg(verus_keep_ghost)`-gated), and
19. //   * not be available on the generic exec `impl<T: Address> ...` blocks (and
20. //     would break `region.rs`, which uses `PageAligned<T>: Address` for a bare
21. //     `T: Address`).
22. // It is left uninterpreted here; the exec contracts pin it operationally
23. // (`into_raw_value` returns exactly `self@`), exactly as the sibling
24. // `FrameAddress::into_raw_value` trust boundary draws the same newtype-identity
25. // fact for the concrete frame address. It is `cfg(verus_keep_ghost)`-gated
26. // (ghost-only), so it does not exist in a normal build.
27. 
28. verus! {
29. 
30. // Ghost projection of any address to its abstract value (`int`).
31. pub uninterp spec fn spec_addr<T: Address>(addr: &T) -> int;
32. 
33. // `<PageAligned<T> as Address>::into_raw_value` is a method of the external
34. // `sys::mm::Address` trait. A trait-impl method cannot be body-verified in place
35. // without marking the whole `impl Address for PageAligned<T>` verified, which
36. // pulls every sibling method into scope and currently triggers a Verus
37. // front-end limitation (`vir/src/traits.rs` assertion). It is therefore specced
38. // here with `assume_specification`, mirroring the trust boundary the codebase
39. // already draws for `<PageAligned<T> as Address>::from_raw_value`
40. // (`kframe.spec.rs`) and `::arch::mem::PAGE_SIZE` (`frame.rs`). The bound is
41. // exactly `T: Address` (matching the external signature), and the `@`-based
42. // contract is expressible because `PageAligned<T>: View` now holds for every
43. // `T: Address`. The real proof obligation is the inner
44. // `<T as Address>::into_raw_value` newtype identity, discharged when the
45. // `Address` trait itself is verified.
46. //
47. // Pure newtype identity projection: the returned raw `usize` is exactly the
48. // abstract address. Callers' in-page offset math and page walking require an
49. // identity projection (no masking/shifting).
50. pub assume_specification<T: Address> [
51.     <PageAligned<T> as Address>::into_raw_value
52. ](addr: PageAligned<T>) -> (result: usize)
53.     ensures
54.         result as int == addr@,
55. ;
56. 
57. } // verus!
58.

# guardrails.py. Substring matching on raw source text was producing
# false positives whenever a function body contained a comment that
# merely *mentioned* `external_body`, `admit()`, or `assume(...)`.
#
# Detection rules (per issue):
#   admit          : a call_expression whose callee is exactly the
#                    identifier `admit` inside the function body.
#   assume         : an assume_expression node, OR a call_expression to
#                    `assume` / `assume_` / `verus_builtin::assume_`
#                    (matched via guardrails._is_assume_axiom_call).
#   external_body  : an attribute_item node whose text contains both a
#                    verus-side keyword (`verifier` or `verus_verify`)
#                    and the literal `external_body`. Reported on the
#                    next item (function_item or struct_item).
#   trusted        : same rule as external_body for the `trusted` token.
#
# Items reported:
#   - function_item with attribute or body issues
#   - struct_item with attribute issues (e.g. external_body wrapper types)
#   - external_body on items annotated with #[verifier::external_type_specification]
#     is annotated as `external_type_spec` so reviewers can scope-check.
get_cheating_detail() {
    local scan_dir="$1"
    VERUS_AI_DIR="$VERUS_AI_DIR" CHEATING_DIR="$scan_dir" python3 -c '
import sys, os
sys.path.insert(0, os.environ["VERUS_AI_DIR"])
from pathlib import Path
from guardrails import _get_parser, _find_nodes, _is_assume_axiom_call, _sibling_has_attr

parser = _get_parser()

ATTR_PATTERNS = {
    "external_body": "external_body",
    "trusted": "trusted",
    "no_decreases": "exec_allows_no_decreases_clause",
}

def collect_preceding_attrs(item_node):
    """Return a list of attribute_item AST nodes immediately preceding the item."""
    attrs = []
    sib = item_node.prev_sibling
    while sib is not None and sib.type in ("attribute_item", "inner_attribute_item"):
        attrs.insert(0, sib)
        sib = sib.prev_sibling
    return attrs

def attr_issue_kinds(attr_node):
    """Return the list of issue kinds an attribute_item declares (verus-side only)."""
    text = attr_node.text.decode()
    if "verifier" not in text and "verus_verify" not in text:
        return []
    kinds = []
    for key, pattern in ATTR_PATTERNS.items():
        if pattern in text:
            kinds.append(key)
    return kinds

def fn_body_admit_lines(fn_node):
    body = fn_node.child_by_field_name("body")
    if body is None:
        return []
    lines = []
    for call in _find_nodes(body, "call_expression"):
        if not call.children:
            continue
        callee = call.children[0]
        if callee.text and callee.text.decode().strip() == "admit":
            lines.append(call.start_point[0] + 1)
    return lines

def fn_body_assume_lines(fn_node):
    body = fn_node.child_by_field_name("body")
    if body is None:
        return []
    lines = []
    # Verus grammar parses `assume(P)` as assume_expression.
    for ax in _find_nodes(body, "assume_expression"):
        lines.append(ax.start_point[0] + 1)
    # Direct calls to verus_builtin::assume_ (and aliases).
    for call in _find_nodes(body, "call_expression"):
        if not call.children:
            continue
        callee = call.children[0]
        if not callee.text:
            continue
        is_axiom, _is_underscore = _is_assume_axiom_call(callee.text.decode())
        if is_axiom:
            lines.append(call.start_point[0] + 1)
    return lines

def is_external_type_spec(item_node):
    for attr in collect_preceding_attrs(item_node):
        text = attr.text.decode()
        if "external_type_specification" in text:
            return True
    return False

for rs_file in sorted(Path(os.environ["CHEATING_DIR"]).glob("**/*.rs")):
    try:
        code = rs_file.read_bytes()
    except OSError:
        continue
    tree = parser.parse(code)

`from_frame_number`, `from_raw_value`) must relate a `PhysicalAddress`'s
`@`-based guarantees (used by `PhysicalAddress::from_number` /

`PageAligned<T>::view`, `PageAligned::from_address`, and `Deref::deref`). The two
projections denote the same integer (the physical address), but the equality is
**not derivable** with the current encoding: `spec_addr<T: Address>` is `uninterp`
(it must be generic over a bare `T: Address`, which carries no `View<V = int>`
bound), and the only fact relating it to a view — the `<PageAligned<T> as
Deref>::deref` boundary (`spec_addr(result) == addr@`) — is tautological once
`PageAligned<T>::view == spec_addr(&self.0)` is unfolded. The identity is therefore
an external-bottom trust boundary that becomes derivable only when the
`sys::mm::Address` trait `impl for PhysicalAddress` is itself verified (blocked
today by its `usize as *const/*mut u8` sibling casts — see
`verus-ai-logs/verus-unsupported.md`). The specification phase reviewed the claim
as semantically sound and deferred it; the proving phase discharges it with the
governed `axiom fn` mechanism (no `admit`, no `external_body`). It states only a
